opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think environmental uncertainty is one of the most underrated axes of difficulty. When people talk about how hard a task is, they usually mean something like "how many reasoning steps does it take" or "how much expertise do you need." Those matter, but a lot of what actually makes a task hard for a model is how much it doesn't know about the world it's operating in, and how much it has to go figure out on its own.

Compare a well-specified math problem with something like "fix this bug in our codebase." With the math problem, everything you need is on the page. The difficulty is all internal: can you reason your way to the answer? With the bug, the model doesn't know the structure of the repo, the conventions the team uses, which tests are flaky, or what the person asking actually cares about. Before it can do the "smart" part, it has to resolve a lot of uncertainty about the environment.

So the way I think about it is roughly in two parts. One is the intrinsic difficulty of the problem once you have full information. The other is how much information gathering, exploration, and hypothesis testing it takes to get to that point. A lot of real-world tasks are pretty easy along the first axis and quite hard along the second. And models have historically been much better at the first than the second. They're great when you hand them everything, and less good at knowing what they don't know, deciding what to look at next, and noticing when an assumption they made five steps ago was wrong.

That also shapes how I think about evaluation. If your benchmarks are mostly fully specified, closed-world problems, you can see really impressive numbers that don't translate into usefulness on messy, open-ended tasks. You're measuring reasoning in a vacuum, while the bottleneck in practice is often calibrated exploration: asking the right clarifying question, running the right command to check something, being appropriately uncertain instead of confidently barreling ahead.

The last piece is that environmental uncertainty interacts with the length of the task. On a short task, a wrong assumption costs you a little. On a long, agentic task, a wrong assumption early on compounds, and you can end up very far from where you should be. So as we push models toward longer-horizon work, I think the ability to manage that uncertainty, by gathering information efficiently, tracking what you believe and why, and revising when the environment pushes back, becomes one of the main things that determines whether a model is actually capable or just looks capable on paper.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fully specified math problems with environmental exploration, but it does not identify pure factual-recall tasks or state that they require no interaction with an environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated dimensions of what makes a task hard. When people talk about task difficulty, they usually reach for things like "how many steps does it take" or "how much reasoning is required," and those matter. But a huge amount of what makes real-world tasks hard isn't the reasoning, it's that the model doesn't actually know the state of the world it's operating in.

So take something like a coding task. If I hand a model a perfectly specified problem with a clean repo and tell it exactly which function to modify, that's one thing. But a real engineer's task looks more like: there's a bug somewhere, the repo is messy, there are three config files and two of them are stale, the tests pass locally but fail in CI for reasons nobody's written down. The hard part isn't writing the fix. The hard part is figuring out what's actually true about the environment before you can even define what the fix should be.

And I think the way I've come to think about it is that difficulty has at least two axes. One is the depth of the reasoning or the length of the horizon. The other is how much of the relevant information is hidden from you at the start and has to be discovered through interaction. A task can be shallow in reasoning but brutal in uncertainty, like debugging a flaky system, or deep in reasoning but fully observable, like a hard math problem. Models have gotten really good at the second kind. The first kind is where I think the gap to a competent human still shows up most clearly.

Part of why that's hard is that handling uncertainty well requires a kind of epistemic discipline. You need to know what you don't know, decide what's worth checking, actually go check it, and update. Humans do this almost without thinking. Models historically have had a strong pull toward just assuming a plausible version of the world and barreling ahead, because that's what looks confident and what often got rewarded in training. So when we evaluate, I care a lot about whether the environment is actually hiding things from the model, and whether the model's behavior changes appropriately when it is. If an eval has no hidden state, you're really only measuring one axis, and you might come away overconfident about how ready the system is for the messy version of the task.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts hidden-state tasks with fully observable hard math problems, but never identifies pure factual-recall tasks or says they require no environmental interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think environmental uncertainty is a really important axis of task difficulty, separate from how much reasoning the task requires. You can have a very hard problem where all the information you need is in the prompt and the rules are clear. But you can also have a seemingly simple task where you don’t know the state of the world, what tools are available, or whether an action actually worked.

In that second case, the model has to do more than come up with a good plan. It has to take an action, observe what happened, update its understanding, and potentially change course. If you’re working in a codebase, for example, the first change you make might reveal that your assumption about how the system works was wrong. Making progress means recognizing that and adapting.

So I’d be careful about using the number of steps alone as a measure of difficulty. A long sequence of predictable steps can be easier than a short task that requires resolving uncertainty. The interesting question is how much the model has to discover along the way, and how well it can recover when the environment contradicts its expectations.

r001.rationale: The response describes tasks whose needed information is in the prompt and rules are clear, but it does not identify pure factual-recall tasks or say they require no environmental interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful distinction is between uncertainty about what to do and uncertainty about what will happen when you do it. A task can require a lot of reasoning but take place in a very predictable environment. And another task can sound simple, but you don’t know the state of the world, your actions might fail, and you have to interpret feedback as you go.

So I wouldn’t measure difficulty just by how many steps the ideal solution takes. I’d also ask: How much can the model observe? How reliable are its actions? And if something goes wrong, can it detect that and recover? A long sequence of predictable steps can be easier than a short sequence where every action introduces uncertainty.

That makes the ability to revise a plan really important. You want a model that can act, check what actually happened, and update its understanding, rather than assuming the environment followed the plan.

r001.rationale: The response discusses environmental uncertainty, action reliability, and feedback, but never identifies pure factual-recall tasks or says they require no environmental interaction to answer correctly.
